name: Jackson Pr. 2.6: two spheres
description: Jackson Problem 2.6: two conducting spheres, one charged, one neutral. Each sphere's charge induces an image in the other, which induces an image in the first, and so on: the neutral sphere becomes a dipole facing the charged one, and both respond to your charges and to the particle itself. Bring the beam into the detector.

reality.represents: Two conducting spheres: images of images (Jackson Pr. 2.6)

remarks.detail: The metal's induced charge is the exact image series plus a fitted surface charge, its boundary error below 1e-10: the conductor is an exact equipotential.

remarks.line: The neutral sphere becomes a dipole
remarks.detail: Each sphere's charge induces an image in the other, and so on: the neutral one polarizes towards the charged one, and both answer your charges and the particle.
The particle pulls on them as hard as they push on it, but they stay put, as if infinitely heavy. Real instruments shape their fields with electrodes held at set voltages, not with point charges.

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
